## Overview

The screenplay is the **audio-first, scene-oriented** intermediate
representation that sits between your technical knowledge and the rendered audio.
It must be renderable by an AI audio producer, human actors, or conventional
studio work — and it must be useful *independently* of the renderer.

This lesson teaches the fundamental constraint of audio writing and the format
of a scene-oriented screenplay.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Explain the constraint "If the listener cannot hear it, it does not exist."
- Distinguish a visual screenplay from an audio screenplay.
- Write scene blocks with AMBIENCE, NARRATOR, dialogue, and SFX.
- Design a sound vocabulary where each sound represents a technical event.
- Use narration, dialogue, pacing, transitions, and fourth-wall breaks
  deliberately.
- Describe the screenplay as an intermediate representation in the production
  pipeline.

## The fundamental constraint

> **If the listener cannot hear it, it does not exist.**

In a visual screenplay, staging can show actions the ear would miss. In audio,
every important action must reach the ear through at least one of:

- **Dialogue** — characters say what is happening.
- **Narration** — the narrator describes what cannot be shown.
- **Sound effect (SFX)** — a sound marks an event.
- **Ambience** — background environment tells the listener where they are.
- **Music** — a cue signals tone, tension, or transition.

If an action is important and none of these carry it, the listener will miss it.
That is the discipline of audio writing.

## Visual vs. audio screenplay

| Visual screenplay | Audio screenplay |
| --- | --- |
| "The chef places the ticket beside the stove." | NARRATOR: "The chef tears the ticket from the rail." [SFX: paper tearing] |
| Camera shows the kitchen | AMBIENCE: "Busy restaurant kitchen." |
| A character glances at the door | NARRATOR: "The manager notices something is wrong." |

The visual version relies on what the eye can see. The audio version must make
every detail audible.

## The scene-oriented format

Each scene block in the screenplay contains:

```
## SCENE 01 — THE TITLE

**LOCATION:** [where the scene takes place]
**AMBIENCE:** [background environment]

**NARRATOR:** [connective narration]

**CHARACTER:** (voice note) [dialogue]

**SFX:** [sound effect that marks an event]

**NARRATOR:** [closing narration — the learning outcome]
```

### Rules

- One scene per `## SCENE` block.
- AMBIENCE goes first — it tells the listener where they are.
- NARRATOR lines carry the explanation that no character voice handles.
- Dialogue carries relationships and state transitions.
- SFX marks specific technical events (see the sound vocabulary below).
- Every scene ends with a closing narration that restates the learning outcome.

## Semantic sound design

Sound effects are not decoration. Each one represents an event or state in the
technical model. Build a **sound vocabulary** early — a table mapping events to
sounds:

| Event / state | Sound |
| --- | --- |
| Request submitted | Ticket printer |
| Template / recipe selected | Book opening |
| Components created | Preparation sounds |
| Provider operation | Appliance hum |
| Successful reconciliation | Service bell |
| Reconciliation failure | Alarm or interruption |

When the listener hears the ticket printer, they know a request was submitted —
without anyone saying so. This is **semantic sound design**: sound as part of the
model.

## Narration and dialogue

- **Use dialogue for relationships and state transitions.** Dialogue shows the
  hand-off between responsibilities: "One application environment, please." →
  "Certainly — I will use the recipe for that order."
- **Use narration for connective tissue.** Narration explains what no character
  voice can carry: the learning outcome, context changes, and the technical
  takeaway.
- **Reserve narration for scene openings and closings.** The opening narration
  sets context; the closing narration states the learning outcome.

## Pacing, transitions, and fourth-wall breaks

- **Pacing.** Give the listener time to absorb each learning outcome. Pause
  before closing narration. Do not rush the final lines of a scene.
- **Transitions.** End each scene on a note that leads into the next — a
  question, a handoff, or a sound that bridges scenes.
- **Fourth-wall breaks.** Occasionally a character may acknowledge its technical
  counterpart ("Hello Developer — ahum, I mean Customer"). Use sparingly. It
  re-anchors the listener when the metaphor risks becoming too entertaining and
  they forget the mapping.

## The screenplay as intermediate representation

The screenplay sits between knowledge and the rendered audio artifact:

```
SOURCE MODEL
Architecture / Documentation / Schemas
        |
TRANSFORMATION
Technical model (concept.md)
Metaphor (metaphor.md)
Characters (characters.md)
Scenes (scenes.md)
        |
INTERMEDIATE REPRESENTATION
screenplay.md
        |
RENDERERS
Wondercraft / Other AI audio / Human actors / Studio
        |
ARTIFACT
audio-play.mp3
```

This means the screenplay must stay useful independently of the renderer. A
screenplay written for Wondercraft should also be usable by human actors or
another AI system without modification.

Read the full screenplay at
[`reference-example/screenplay.md`](../../reference-example/screenplay.md).

## Writing your screenplay.md

For each scene in your `scenes.md`, write a screenplay block that carries the
scene's action through dialogue, narration, and sound. Remember:

- If an event is important, make it audible.
- If a relationship matters, put it in dialogue.
- If the learning outcome needs restating, use closing narration.
- If a sound marks a technical event, use the sound vocabulary.
